Everyday Tech Secrets: the Big Doc

54 documented cases. Safety and legal note: only try things on devices and accounts you own, and check each source before acting.

Raspberry Pi

1. Pi-hole: block ads for your whole house

Raspberry PiEasyskill: Low

Pi-hole is free software that runs on a small Raspberry Pi connected to your home router. It works as a filter for web addresses, so requests to known ad and tracking servers are blocked for every device on your network. At home it cleans up ads on phones, smart TVs and laptops without installing anything on each one. For anyone at home it means fewer ads and less tracking with one setup. The catch is that some sites and apps can break, so keep a backup DNS setting handy.

Source: https://notes.aliciasykes.com/23239/top-25-raspberry-pi-projects

2. RetroPie: turn a Pi into an arcade

Raspberry PiEasyskill: Low

RetroPie is a ready-made software image for a Raspberry Pi that turns it into a retro game console. You write the image to an SD card, plug the Pi into a TV, and play classic games using a regular controller. It is a cheap family project and a fun way to learn about computers. The software is legal, but downloading game files (ROMs) you do not own is not.

Source: https://tech.yahoo.com/articles/7-projects-might-finally-raspberry-130015396.html

3. Home Assistant on a Pi: one brain for the whole smart home

Raspberry PiMediumskill: Low

Home Assistant is free software that runs on a Pi and links smart lights, locks, cameras and TVs into one system. You can make devices react to each other, such as dimming lights when a show starts, and much of it works locally without the cloud. People like having one dashboard instead of many separate apps. The source says a Pi with at least 2GB of RAM is needed and that a ready-made image is available in Raspberry Pi Imager. Expect some setup time.

Source: https://tech.yahoo.com/computing/articles/7-raspberry-pi-projects-1-130016464.html

4. Kiwix hotspot: Wikipedia with no internet

Raspberry PiMediumskill: Low

Kiwix lets a Raspberry Pi create its own Wi-Fi network that serves a saved copy of Wikipedia to nearby phones. It works with no internet connection, because the content is downloaded ahead of time. It suits classrooms, clinics, camping trips or places with weak signal. The catch is that the content files are large and the copy is only as fresh as your last download.

Source: https://kiwix.org/en/applications/

5. Pi flight tracker (PiAware)

Raspberry PiMediumskill: Low

PiAware is a Raspberry Pi setup that receives the radio signals planes broadcast about their position and shows them live on a map. It needs a Pi, a small antenna and a cheap USB radio dongle. It is a good hobby project for aviation fans and a fun way to see what flies over your home. Receiving these signals is legal in most places, but check your local rules. The source is a wiki page, so details may vary by version.

Source: https://wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Piaware

6. tar1090: a pro grade plane radar page for your Pi

Raspberry PiMediumskill: Low

tar1090 is a free web page you add to a Pi plane tracker that shows aircraft with trails, history and callsigns, like a mini air traffic screen. It reads from the same radio dongle your tracker already uses. Hobbyists and engineers use it to get a clearer, more detailed view of nearby flights. The catch is that only one decoder program should use the radio dongle at a time.

Source: https://guide.airframes.io/ads-b/installation/recommended/tar1090

7. Hyperion: DIY Ambilight for any TV

Raspberry PiMediumskill: Low

Hyperion drives an LED strip behind your TV so the wall glows in the colors of what is on screen, similar to Philips Ambilight. A Pi takes the video through a capture dongle and tells the lights what to show. It makes movies and games feel bigger for a modest cost. The catch is that you must buy the LED strip hardware, and streaming apps with copy protection may block the capture.

Source: https://peyanski.com/home-assistant-hyperion-integration-how-to/

8. MotionEye: Pi as a security camera hub

Raspberry PiMediumskill: Low

MotionEye turns a Raspberry Pi and a cheap camera into a home security camera system with motion detection and alerts. Footage stays in your hands instead of a monthly subscription service. It can watch a door, a garage or a pet while you are out. The catch is legal: check local laws on recording people, especially audio, and keep the system password protected.

Source: https://notes.aliciasykes.com/23239/top-25-raspberry-pi-projects

smart TV

9. Turn off the TV tracking settings

smart TVEasyskill: None

Smart TVs have privacy settings, including ACR (automatic content recognition), that limit what the TV tracks about your viewing. Anyone with a smart TV can use this to cut down on data collected about their household. It takes a few minutes in the settings menu. The catch is that menu names and options differ by brand and model.

Source: https://news.yahoo.com/turn-off-smart-tv-snooping-060657238.html

10. Sideload any app on a Fire TV with Downloader

smart TVEasyskill: Low

Downloader is an app on Amazon Fire TV that lets you type a web address and install apps that Amazon does not list. You first flip one setting that allows installs from unknown sources. It is useful for tools like file managers or custom launchers. The catch is that you should only install apps you trust, because pirated streaming apps are risky and illegal.

Source: https://www.aftvnews.com/?p=18235

11. Strip ads and bloat from a TV with ADB

smart TVMediumskill: Low

This project uses ADB (a developer tool that talks to Android devices from a computer) to disable ad and tracking apps on an Android TV. The source says to disable packages rather than uninstall them, back up the package list first, and turn ADB debugging off when you are done. It can make the TV cleaner for people comfortable with a command line. It applies to Android TVs only. The catch is that disabling the wrong packages can cause problems.

Source: https://itsfoss.com/news/debloat-smart-tv/

12. Control a Roku from code with ECP

smart TVMediumskill: Low

Roku's ECP (External Control Protocol) is an official interface that lets a script or button send remote-control commands to a Roku over your home network. Engineers can use it to automate play, pause or app launching. Hobbyists use it to build custom remotes or smart-home actions. The source notes newer Roku OS versions need the Control by mobile apps setting enabled.

Source: https://developer.roku.com/dev/docs/external-control-api

13. Roku in Home Assistant

smart TVEasyskill: Low

Home Assistant can detect a Roku on your network and add it automatically. Once connected, you can make other things react to it, such as dimming lights when you press play. It brings the TV into the same smart-home system as your other devices. The source is a third-party page, so check the official documentation for current steps.

Source: https://selorahomes.com/home-assistant/integrations/roku/

14. LG TV rooting with the Homebrew Channel

smart TVAdvancedskill: High

Security researchers found ways to unlock certain LG TVs so they run community apps that LG never approved, through the Homebrew Channel project. It lets owners add features and take more control of the TV. The catch is that LG does not support it, it may void the warranty, and many firmwares have been patched, so check firmware status first.

Source: https://webosbrew.org

home camera

15. Scrypted bridges Wyze cams into HomeKit

home cameraAdvancedskill: High

Scrypted is a free hub that can show cameras in the Apple Home app. The linked guide uses Wyze cameras flashed with the Dafang-Hack custom firmware, so it means replacing the camera's own firmware. That makes it an advanced project with some risk of breaking the camera. It is a fit for Apple users who want all their cameras in one app. The setup is community work and not supported by Wyze or Apple.

Source: https://github.com/koush/scrypted/wiki/Wyze

16. ring-mqtt: Ring doorbell in Home Assistant

home cameraMediumskill: Low

ring-mqtt connects a Ring doorbell to smart-home systems like Home Assistant. That lets the doorbell trigger actions such as flashing lights or announcing a visitor. It is handy for people who want their devices to work together. The catch is that it is unofficial, uses your Ring login, and may break if Ring changes its service.

Source: https://github.com/tsightler/ring-mqtt/wiki

17. Eufy cameras in Home Assistant

home cameraMediumskill: Low

This is a community add-on that brings Eufy cameras and doorbells into Home Assistant. It lets you see and automate them with the rest of your smart home. It suits people who want one dashboard for everything. The catch is that it is unofficial, features are limited and it may stop working after Eufy changes its app.

Source: https://github.com/fuatakgun/eufy_security

18. Wyze camera to local only with Thingino

home cameraAdvancedskill: High

Thingino is open-source firmware that can replace the software on a Wyze camera so that footage stays inside your house. It suits people who want a local-only camera. The catch is that you lose the Wyze cloud and there is a risk of bricking the camera. Only do this on cameras you own.

Source: https://thingino.com

Automobile

19. Openpilot turns a regular car into a self-steering assistant

AutomobileMediumskill: Low

Openpilot is free open-source driver-assistance software that runs on a small device from comma. It can add lane keeping and highway steering help to hundreds of ordinary cars (the page says 300 plus). It is of interest to drivers and engineers curious about how car assistance works. The catch is that you need the comma device, you stay fully responsible as the driver, and it may affect your warranty or insurance.

Source: https://github.com/commaai/openpilot

20. Tesla API reverse engineered by owners

AutomobileMediumskill: Low

Tesla owners and fans documented how the Tesla mobile app talks to the car, so anyone can write code to check charge or pre-heat the car. It lets hobbyists build their own automations and dashboards. The catch is that this is unofficial, Tesla has changed the interface over time, and you should never share your login token.

Source: https://github.com/timdorr/model-s-api

21. Kia and Hyundai in Home Assistant

AutomobileMediumskill: Low

An open-source add-on shows a Kia or Hyundai's battery, door locks and location inside a Home Assistant smart-home dashboard. Owners can check on the car from the same screen as the rest of the house. The catch is that it is unofficial and may break when Kia or Hyundai change their app service.

Source: https://github.com/Hyundai-Kia-Connect/kia_uvo

22. Car Scanner app reads hidden car data

AutomobileEasyskill: Low

Car Scanner is a free phone app that pairs with a cheap Bluetooth OBD2 adapter plugged into your car. It shows live data such as engine, battery and temperature numbers that the dashboard hides, and can read warning codes. It helps drivers and mechanics understand a problem before paying for diagnosis. You need the small adapter, with no soldering. Read-only use is safe, but changing coded settings can cause faults.

Source: https://www.carscanner.info/

23. Hidden feature coding for VW, Audi, Skoda, Toyota via app

AutomobileMediumskill: Medium

Car Scanner supports coding hidden settings on some Volkswagen group cars (VW, Audi, Skoda and Seat) on the MQB, PQ26 and MLB-EVO platforms. It appeals to owners who like to customize their cars. Coding can cause faults or affect your warranty, so back up the original settings first. Compatibility depends on the exact model.

Source: https://www.carscanner.info/

Smartphone

24. Secret testing menu with a dial code

SmartphoneEasyskill: None

Typing *#*#4636#*#* into the phone dialer on some Android phones opens a hidden testing screen. It shows phone, usage and network details, which is handy for troubleshooting. Curious users can use it to check a phone before buying or fixing it. The catch is that it varies by brand, and you should not change settings you do not understand.

Source: https://www.androidcentral.com/apps-software/best-secret-android-settings

25. Secret Android settings you can turn on

SmartphoneEasyskill: None

Android Central lists hidden Android settings that most people never find. Turning some on can make a phone easier to use or more private. It is useful for anyone who wants to tweak their phone without extra apps. The risk is low, but change one thing at a time so you can undo a problem.

Source: https://www.androidcentral.com/apps-software/best-secret-android-settings

26. Make your phone feel faster with one hidden setting

SmartphoneEasyskill: None

Developer Options on Android lets you halve the animation times, which can make many phones feel snappier. It costs nothing and takes a minute. It helps anyone with an older or slower phone. The catch is that it is safe and reversible, but Developer Options being on can upset some banking apps.

Source: https://tech.yahoo.com/computing/articles/hidden-setting-sped-android-phone-160015078.html

27. Debloat your phone without root

SmartphoneMediumskill: Low

Universal Android Debloater is a free desktop tool that removes pre-installed junk apps from a phone through ADB, without rooting it. Removing them can free storage and reduce background activity. It suits people who are comfortable connecting a phone to a computer. The catch is that this original repo is no longer maintained, so use the community fork Universal Android Debloater Next Generation, and removing system parts can break the phone.

Source: https://github.com/0x192/universal-android-debloater

28. Old Android phone becomes a home web server

SmartphoneMediumskill: Medium

Termux is an Android app that gives a terminal where an old phone can run a small website or file share. This turns a drawer phone into a tiny always-on computer for hobby or learning projects. Keep it on your home network and use passwords. Watch battery safety and heat, because a phone left plugged in around the clock can swell its battery.

Source: https://en.androidayuda.com/How-to-create-a-web-server-on-your-old-Android-phone/

29. Old phone becomes a Jellyfin movie server

SmartphoneMediumskill: Medium

An old Android phone can run Jellyfin through Termux to stream your own video files to the TV, with Samba for file sharing. It repurposes a spare device as a media server. The catch is to only stream media you own, and Android may stop background apps to save power.

Source: https://medium.com/@wasiqmansoor/building-an-adroid-based-home-server-with-termux-jellyfin-and-samba-64a9aa9d33cb

30. Old phones as cheap security cameras

SmartphoneEasyskill: Low

An old phone's camera can be reused to monitor a pet, a door or a 3D printer. The linked page lists a camera stream as a possible use, with heat and privacy as the main limits. It saves buying a dedicated camera and gives a second life to old hardware. Do not film where people expect privacy, protect it with passwords, and watch for battery swelling.

Source: https://shop.zimaspace.com/blogs/support-tips/can-an-old-android-phone-become-a-home-server

Apps

31. HTTP Toolkit: easier traffic inspection

AppsMediumskill: Medium

HTTP Toolkit is a friendlier tool for inspecting the web requests an app or device makes. Engineers use it to see what data an app sends and to debug problems. It can also help a curious person check what an app shares. The catch is to use it on your own devices only, and installing its certificate lowers security while it is active.

Source: https://blog.openreplay.com/inspecting-https-requests-http-toolkit/

32. Instaloader downloads Instagram profiles

AppsMediumskill: Low

Instaloader is a free script that can save photos, stories and captions from Instagram profiles you can access. It can be used for backing up your own account. Mass downloading may break Instagram's terms and accounts can be restricted. Only use it on your own account, and respect copyright and other people's privacy.

Source: https://github.com/instaloader/instaloader

33. Spicetify customizes Spotify

AppsMediumskill: Low

Spicetify is a tool that reskins and extends the Spotify desktop app with custom themes and extensions. It lets users personalize how Spotify looks and behaves. The catch is that third-party mods can break after updates and may breach Spotify's terms.

Source: https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/spotify

34. Unofficial FlightRadar24 tools

AppsMediumskill: Medium

Open-source wrappers let code read live plane positions from FlightRadar24. Hobbyists and engineers can use them to build their own tracking pages. The catch is that this is for educational use only, and commercial use needs permission.

Source: https://github.com/JeanExtreme002/FlightRadarAPI

35. Librespot: Spotify without the official app

AppsAdvancedskill: High

Librespot is open-source code that lets other devices play Spotify Premium through their own player rather than the official app. It helps hobbyists put Spotify on speakers and gadgets. The catch is that it needs Premium, is likely against Spotify's terms, and may break when authentication changes.

Source: https://github.com/librespot-org/librespot/wiki

36. Baileys: WhatsApp without the app

AppsAdvancedskill: High

Baileys is a library that lets programs send and receive WhatsApp messages as a linked device. Developers use it to build bots and automations. The catch is that it is unofficial, spam use gets numbers banned, and it is not affiliated with WhatsApp.

Source: https://www.mintlify.com/whiskeysockets/Baileys

Privacy fails and news stories (not hacking projects)

These are real events and findings to learn from. They are not projects to try, so they carry no skill rating.

37. Smart TVs collect viewing data even as external screens

smart TV

Researchers at UC3M reported that smart TVs collect viewing data even when the TV is used only as an external screen. This matters for anyone who plugs a laptop or console into a smart TV. The source is a short press release.

Source: https://alphagalileo.org/en-gb/Item-Display/ItemId/253112

38. Eufy owners see other people's homes

home camera

In May 2021, Eufy camera owners reported seeing strangers' camera feeds in their apps. Users later said the issue appeared resolved. It shows how a software fault at the company can expose private video without any hacking by the owner. Anyone with a home camera can learn to check settings and watch for company notices.

Source: https://inverse.com/input/culture/eufy-security-camera-owners-reporting-seeing-other-users-homes

39. Non-standard smartphone wiretapping explained

Smartphone

Kaspersky gives a plain explanation of non-standard ways a phone can be used to listen in, using its sensors rather than the microphone. It helps people understand what is possible and how to reduce risk. The page is a blog explainer and not a how-to.

Source: https://www.kaspersky.com/blog/non-standard-smartphone-wiretapping/

40. Strava heatmap exposed secret military bases

Apps

In 2018 Strava's public heatmap lit up the running and cycling paths of soldiers at hidden bases around the world. The lesson is that harmless-looking public data can reveal sensitive locations when combined. Anyone who uses a fitness app can check their own privacy zones. The catch is that this is a real historical case, not a how-to.

Source: https://www.singletracks.com/uncategorized/stravas-global-heatmap-may-reveal-secret-military-bases-around-world/

41. Snapchat 4.6 million usernames leak

Apps

Snapchat had been warned about a weakness by Gibson Security. In 2013 a site then published about 4.6 million usernames with partly hidden phone numbers. It shows why companies should act on security reports and why users should limit what an app knows about them. This is a historic case.

Source: https://techcrunch.com/2013/12/31/hackers-claim-to-publish-list-of-4-6m-snapchat-usernames-and-numbers/

42. Venmo payments were public by default

Apps

Venmo payments were public by default, so one researcher scraped about 7 million of them, showing who paid whom and why. Anyone who uses Venmo can learn from this to check their privacy setting. The catch is that mass scraping like this is controversial.

Source: https://www.securityweek.com/researcher-scrapes-and-posts-7-million-venmo-transactions

43. TikTok and 53 apps read your clipboard

Apps

When Apple's iOS 14 added a clipboard warning, it showed that TikTok and 53 other apps were reading whatever the user had last copied. TikTok said the reads came from an anti spam feature and promised to remove it. The takeaway is to keep passwords and private text out of the clipboard.

Source: https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/ios-14-flags-tiktok-53-other-apps-spying-on-iphone-clipboards

44. 99 phones fake a Google Maps traffic jam

Apps

An artist pulled a wagon with 99 phones through a quiet Berlin street and made Google Maps show it as a traffic jam. It shows how crowd location data can be fooled by a simple trick. The catch is that it could divert real drivers and is not recommended to repeat.

Source: https://tomsguide.com/news/99-smartphones-google-maps-hack

45. Uber 2022 breach via tired approval taps

Apps

In the 2022 Uber breach, an attacker kept sending login approval requests until the contractor accepted one, a pattern often called MFA fatigue. The lesson for everyone is never to approve a login you did not start, and to report repeated prompts. The source is an SEC filing.

Source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1543151/000155278122000558/e22427_ex99-1.htm

46. CIA Weeping Angel: the fake off TV

smart TV

Documents leaked in 2017 described a CIA tool called Weeping Angel, which could fake an off state on a Samsung F8000 TV while it kept listening. The documents mention infection by USB drive. It shows how an always-connected device can be turned against its owner. This is a news story and not a project to try.

Source: https://theintercept.com/2017/03/07/wikileaks-dump-shows-cia-could-turn-smart-tvs-into-listening-devices/

47. Smart TV camera and mic hijack

smart TV

In December 2012, researchers at ReVuln showed that a Samsung smart TV could be taken over from the same network, including its camera and microphone. The practical lesson is to cover TV cameras with a shutter and keep firmware updated. This is an older report, so details of current models differ.

Source: https://www.nbcnews.com/technolog/whos-watching-whom-camera-equipped-tv-can-be-hacked-says-1C7596675

48. Ring doorbell leaked your Wi-Fi password

home camera

Researchers at Bitdefender found that the Ring doorbell's setup process sent your Wi-Fi password in the clear for anyone nearby to capture. It is a good example of why updates matter. The catch is that this was 2019 research and it has been patched.

Source: https://techcrunch.com/2019/11/07/amazon-ring-doorbells-wifi-hackers

49. Ring app live feed interception

home camera

Researchers at BullGuard showed they could intercept and inject fake video into the Ring app's live feed. It shows why security updates for home cameras matter. Ring patched the problem in app version 3.4.7. This was a 2019 demo.

Source: https://threatpost.com/ring-doorbell-flaw-opens-door-to-spying/142265

50. Jeep Cherokee remotely hijacked over the internet

Automobile

Two researchers remotely controlled a Jeep Cherokee's radio, steering, brakes and engine over the internet. Fiat Chrysler issued a patch, and the affected system was in up to 471,000 US vehicles. It showed that connected cars need security as much as phones do. This is a historic case and should never be tried on a vehicle you do not own.

Source: https://techradar.com/news/car-tech/hackers-sabotage-jeep-remotely-1299807

51. Any Kia unlocked with only a license plate

Automobile

Researchers showed that a car's license plate number plus bugs in Kia's systems could be used to remotely control certain Kias. Kia fixed it after the researchers reported it. It is a lesson on why companies should fix reported bugs quickly. Unauthorized access to anyone's car is illegal.

Source: https://samcurry.net/hacking-kia

52. Students unlock paid Tesla features with a voltage trick

Automobile

Researchers at TU Berlin glitched the computer of a Tesla Model 3 to unlock heated rear seats that normally need a $300 purchase. It shows how hardware can be tested for weaknesses. The catch is that it needed soldering and physical access, and unlocking paid features may violate terms.

Source: https://www.theregister.com/2023/08/07/black_hat_tesla_hackers/

53. Phone accelerometer can hear speech

Smartphone

Researchers showed that a phone's motion sensor (accelerometer) can pick up speech played through the phone's own loudspeaker, without microphone permission. It helps security teams understand why sensor access matters. The catch is that it is academic research.

Source: https://www.ndss-symposium.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/24076.pdf

54. Pegasus zero-click iPhone hack

Smartphone

Pegasus is commercial spyware, and one version could infect an iPhone through a message without the owner tapping anything (zero-click). Apple patched the FORCEDENTRY flaw in September 2021 with iOS 14.8. It is a reminder to install updates promptly. The spyware has been used against activists.

Source: https://citizenlab.ca/2021/09/forcedentry-nso-group-imessage-zero-click-exploit-captured-in-the-wild/
